banner: Research context for analyst review — not a trading instruction.

input.raw_text: Shanghai was a horror show again — the circuit breakers got scrapped after the first week, but the selling hasn't stopped, and the composite is back under 3,000 for the first time in more than a year. Oil is what's breaking everything now: WTI has traded under $30 and touched the mid-$20s overnight, and the energy complex is dragging credit and the banks down with it. U.S. equities have given back the entire bounce from Wednesday, and the S&P is now down around ten percent for the year — three weeks in. Nobody wants to be the last one out of the risk trade; even the dip-buyers from December have gone quiet. Gold is catching a real bid, and pricing of a March Fed hike has essentially gone to zero. This feels like de-risking for its own sake.
input.summary: Persistent selling in Chinese equities, sharply depressed oil prices, weakness across energy-linked credit and banks, and renewed losses in U.S. equities indicate broad risk aversion. Gold demand is strengthening, expectations for a March Federal Reserve rate increase have nearly disappeared, and market participation appears dominated by generalized de-risking.

interpretation.summary: The packet strongly describes generalized risk aversion, but none of the retrieved states captures that phenomenon with the evidence supplied. The candidates instead require horizon-specific return dependence, pair convergence, option-spread behavior, fitted regime probabilities, conditional tail correlations, distributional moments, or volatility-persistence statistics. The futures, hedge-fund, and options candidates also fall outside the relevant instrument scope.

observations.statement: Shanghai Composite below 3,000 amid persistent selling
WTI below $30 after touching the mid-$20s
Energy weakness pressuring credit markets and banks
U.S. equities surrendering the prior rebound
S&P down roughly ten percent within three weeks
Risk appetite fading alongside quieter dip-buying activity
March Federal Reserve rate-increase probability near zero
Broad de-risking without a clearly identified incremental catalyst
